hooks.text: Earth pulls the space station with nearly ninety percent of surface gravity.
Astronauts on the space station are actually plunging toward Earth right now.
Why do orbiting astronauts float if Earth's gravity never actually disappeared?

title: Why Astronauts Aren't Actually in Zero Gravity
description: Astronauts aboard the space station are not floating in a zero-gravity void. They are in perpetual free fall around Earth under nearly full planetary gravity.

beats.text: Earth pulls the space station with nearly ninety percent of surface gravity.
beats.visual: Photograph of the International Space Station orbiting high above Earth's curved limb, 2011

beats.text: Most people assume astronauts float weightlessly because Earth's gravity disappears in space.
beats.visual: Astronaut floating freely inside the International Space Station Destiny laboratory, 2007

beats.text: At a normal orbital altitude of four hundred kilometers, gravity still measures eight point seven meters per second squared.
beats.visual: High-altitude photograph of Earth's atmosphere and curvature from low Earth orbit, 2018

beats.text: The sensation of weight does not come from gravity, but from contact forces like floors pushing against your body.
beats.visual: Diagram showing normal contact force pushing back against a person on the ground, 2020

beats.text: Without a supporting force resisting you, apparent weight completely drops to zero.
beats.visual: Interior view of astronauts floating inside the cupola of the space station, 2015

beats.text: Astronauts appear to float because they and the station accelerate downward at the exact same rate.
beats.visual: Illustration of Isaac Newton's cannonball falling around Earth's curved horizon, 1728

beats.text: Immense horizontal speed causes Earth's curved surface to drop away as fast as the spacecraft falls.
beats.visual: Exterior photograph of a satellite speeding over Earth's sunlit horizon, 2021

beats.text: Weightlessness is never the absence of gravity, but an unending fall around the planet.
beats.visual: Wide photograph of the International Space Station in perpetual free fall above blue oceans, 2018
